projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Walter G. Degrange was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: My name is Michael Lyons. I'm co-manager of Echo Range Retirement. I'm here with Walter Degrange, a veteran. And today is November 11th, 2004. It's approximately 3:15 p.m. Walt, is it okay if we tape record this conversation?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yes. Okay with me.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Okay. Thank you.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Okay. We'll start from the beginning.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: You just got done telling me you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: I enlisted in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: In Coraopolis, Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Why did you join?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: I was mad at the Japanese for bombing Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Well, there you go.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Why did you pick the Navy?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Because I've seen all them cartoons of G.I. Joe and guys living at ____ and helmets, and that, and I figured, well, I wanted a cleaner life when I went in, so I joined the Navy.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Well, there you go. Do you recall your first days in the service?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Did I do what?

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Do you recall your first days in the service?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Oh, yeah. It was strange at first. I was never away from home before, so I missed Mom and missed Dad, and all that, but I got used to it after I got acquainted with everybody, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Tell me about your boot camp and training experience.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Oh, boot camp was -- we went through boot camp in six weeks. Used to be 14 weeks, but when I went through, they was rushing them through.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: So, we didn't get too much training, really, you know. And I haven't got no experiences to tell you about there.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Where did you go to boot camp?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Up In Newport, Rhode Island.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Oh, okay. Do you remember any of your instructors there, how they treated you or anything?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Well, this one guy, someone stole something, and they made us stand back there at attention for three or four hours trying to find out who stole, what it was.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Oh, I see.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: So, evidently, this is what I remember.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: So, you got through basic --

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Got basic --

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: -- pretty easy?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Okay. Yes, sure.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: And you were both in World War II and Korea?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Where exactly did you go during World War II?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Well, during World War -- the first ship I got on, we went down to Bermuda. It was an auxillary mine sweeper, and we practiced sweeping mines down in Bermuda. And we come back to the states, and they decommissioned the ship and recommission it as a P.C., a patrol craft, and they put twin forties on it, and we started going out and doing convoy duty for the North Atlantic.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Okay. And after that?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: We went to the Med, went over to Sicily, went over to Oran, Southern France, went up to England, Scotland. I made the rounds, in other words.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Yeah, I guess. You got all over the place.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Do you remember arriving in Europe, and what was it like?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Strange. I'd never been in a foreign country, and it was -- when we first went ashore there, it -- it was a new experience, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Well, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Mm-hm. What was your job as -- or assignment on board?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: I was a quartermaster ____ in charge, helped with navigation and stuff like that.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: I see. Did you see combat?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Well, yeah. We was in the battle of Southern France, yeah. And we patrolled off the -- off the Italian coast and had a German E-boat come up, and we destroyed that, and we picked up a few bodies, you know, the sailors did.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Were there any casualties in your unit on your boat?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: No, no. We never suffered any casualties, no.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Well, that's always good.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Tell me about a couple of your most memorable experiences on board.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Well, I tell you, I was aboard ship, and I had a lot of fun when I was in the Navy. I used to drink an awful lot, and we was coming back off liberty. We was down in Charleston, South Carolina, at the time, and I thought there was a gang plank between the two ships, and there wasn't. I stepped off, and I fell right down in between the ship and had my pea coat on and my blues, and I was sinking fast.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: I'll bet.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: And they threw me a three-inch line, and I got that tied around me, and they called three or four guys from down below, and they come out and they hauled me back up aboard ship.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: A sobering experience, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Very sobering, I'll tell you.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Oh, my, Walter.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: I have all kinds of stories I could tell you.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Give me another one.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah. We was down in Cuba, and I was out on the beach. We were all drinking wine. We went to get some wine, you know. There was a bunch of us guys, and then we bought a couple bottles of wine. We sat on the beach and were drinking wine, and I got real hot, and I said, "I'm going to dive in." I went and dove in, and that's the last thing I remember. When I come out of the water, I didn't have no trunks on, and I'm running down the beach stark naked, all them tourists there, and then the next thing I remember, I'm aboard ship.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: I woke up aboard ship sitting at a dining room table, and I said, "how did I get there?"

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Yeah. You were --

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: I had a lot of fun, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Yeah. And what medals or awards did you receive?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Medals or awards?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Well, just the European Theater and -- well, the Good Conduct, and other than that, nothing else, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: A Bronze Star?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Okay. Let me see. How did you stay in touch with your family? Were you able to?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Just by letters. Just wrote letters home, and that was it. You had to wait two or three weeks before you heard anything, you know. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Mm-hm. What was the food like?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Nothing wrong with the food. The food was good. The Navy really fed you good, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: You always had plenty of supplies and stuff?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: This is the same question that screwed me up on all the interviews. Did you feel pressure or stress? Were you scared at any time, basically?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. You ain't kidding. When that E-boat was coming for us, everybody got scared.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Yeah, I'm sure. I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: It was them or you, right?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah. And I tell you, it's either them or you is right.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Was there ever anything -- was there ever something special that you did for good luck? Did you have a rabbit's foot or --

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Well, you know, we -- I got aboard the DD seventy-seven ninety DH Fox, and we took a world cruise with the USS Huntington, the cruiser, and we left Norfolk, we went over, we went up to England, come in through the Meds, went through the Meds, visited France, Italy, Sicily, Malta, we went down to the Red Sea, went down the other side of Africa, Durban and Capetown, and went from there, come over to South America, Buenos Aires, Brazil, and then come up and hit the Trinidad, and then went to Cuba, and went from Cuba down to Panama, and went over the west end -- on the west side of Panama, come back through and went up, and we ended the cruise up in Norfolk.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: That was -- and we went over the Equator during that, and that's an experience, too, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: I understand they have some sort of a tradition when you go over the Equator for the first time.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah. And they had me -- this quartermaster, the chief quarter, he didn't care for me too much, and he was a Shell Back (ph), and I was a Polliwog, and the day before we went over, they had me up in the -- up in the crow's nest with a roll of toilet paper throwing it up, saying, "I'm a ship bird, I'm a ship bird." That was my initiation.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Oh, God.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, I tell you what they don't do when you get initiated, when you go over the Equator, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Yeah. This probably -- you probably just answered this question, but how did people entertain themselves when they were on board?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Well, we played cards. We played a lot of poker. We played dice, and we played Pinochle and Gin Rummy, and things like that.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Mm-hm. Did you ever get to see any kind of entertainers?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Oh, yes. Bob Hope, yeah. Bob Hope, when we were down in Bermuda, him and his entourage come down there and entertained us. It was real nice, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: That's cool. What did you do when you went on leave?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Just went home and seen Mom and Dad and went to school, see the kids that I -- when I dropped out of school to join the Navy, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Yeah. So, you dropped out of school to join the Navy?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah. And they had me on the honor roll up there in school, the first one that enlisted in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Well, there you go. That's nice.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: It gave me some honor, anyway.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Let me see. Did you guys ever play pranks on each other?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: No. Not too much, not really too much because you're buddy-buddies, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Yeah. What did you think of the officers?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Well, some officers are nice. This one captain, he had it in for me because every time I turned around, he had me in the brig or something for doing something wrong, and I think I was probably excused a couple of times, but he just didn't like me, you know, and he broke -- he busted me one time. We're on this here tanker, and I'm at the wheel, and the carrier's alongside there, and we're in my first class rights, you know, I'm first class quartermaster, and he had took me to captain's mast and busted me, and I'm in there steering, and he looks in there, and he looks at the yeoman there, and he says -- his name was Parley Candriotis (ph) -- he says, "Parley Candriotis," he said, "didn't I bust Mr. DeGrange here?" "Well, yes, Captain, but it's not approved yet." He said, "I want it approved right now. Bust him. Bust him right now." He's hollering, and everybody up in the carrier there, they knew I got busted that day, and he had me relieved off the wheel, and I went down and had to cut the other stripe off and go back up. So, he's the only bad one that I can remember.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Yeah. How about your fellow sailors? A lot of good guys?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Oh, a lot of good guys. A lot of good guys.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Did you keep a personal diary?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Do you remember the day when you got out of the service?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Well, yeah. When I got out, I got out on a military disability at Saint Auburns (ph) Naval Hospital down in New York, and I had got out, and I was making 286 dollars a month. That was my pay.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: That was 1962, you said?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah. So I -- when I got out, I had to look for a job, and I had -- they discharged me with a brace on. I had a back brace on. Because I couldn't run up and down the steps, they just kicked me out of the Navy, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: So, I just come out and I'm trying to get a job. I got a job waiting in a bar, bartender in New York at a hotel, and then they finally -- I had a brother-in-law come up and visited me. He was working the post office, and he said, "Why don't you try and get a job at the post office?" And so put in an application, and they took me, and I was in the post office for 14 years.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah. And I hurt my back in the post office, and I got a disability from the post office, yeah. So, I'm on two disability checks.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Not bad.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Not bad, I tell you.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Did you make any close friendships while you were in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Oh, yeah, I did. But you lose track of them guys. One guy went to Guam, and I never heard from him. The other guy, he got out. A lot of them didn't stay, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Did you join any veterans organizations?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: I belong to the F.R.A., the V.F.A., the Navy Memorial Foundation. I belong to all of them. I belong to the Moose. I'm a life member of the Moose. So, I'm -- but I don't never go to the meetings because they're up in New York and I'm down here.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Yeah. It would be a long trip for the meeting, that's for sure. Did your military experience influence your thinking about war or about the military in general?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah. It -- it -- I learned that you just don't go out and shoot another man because the government tells you to do that because, I mean, you're killing somebody. He don't want to kill you no more than you want to kill him, and you're doing it because the government's telling you to do it, you know. And I just don't go with their policies, but I'm a true American, so you got to go with what the government says, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: I guess. You said you enjoy organizations. Have you ever gone to any of the reunions of the --

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: No, no. I could never afford it. They're always too far away, you know, yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Yeah. How did your service and experiences affect your life? In other words, Walt DeGrange, a kid out of high school going in the Navy, how did it change you?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: It made me -- it made me who I am today. I mean, I like people. I talk to a lot of people. I get along with people, and I'm not what you'd call an educated man, but I did finish high school with a GED.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: But I could have went to college or something like that, but I never did take the opportunity to do that. The G.I. Bill afforded me that, but I didn't take advantage of it, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: I understand.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: I guess we're getting near the end. Is there anything you'd like to add that we've not covered in the interview?

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: No, not really. It's -- not other than I'm glad I'm still here.

sp.speaker: Michael P. Lyons
sp.p: Amen to that, Walt. Well, thank you, very much. And at this point, we will end the interview.

sp.speaker: Walter G. Degrange
sp.p: Okay, good. Thank you, very much.
